title: Bounded complexes belong to triangulated subcategories containing their terms
statement: Let $\mathcal A$ be an abelian category [def-sp-abelian] whose unbounded derived category $D(\mathcal A)$ exists [def-weil-abstract-derived-category]. Let $\mathcal S$ be a strictly full triangulated subcategory of $D(\mathcal A)$ [def-weil-triangulated-category]: it contains zero and is closed under isomorphisms, all integer shifts, and taking the third vertex of a distinguished triangle when the other two vertices belong to it. Let $C^\bullet$ be a cochain complex of objects of $\mathcal A$, and let $a,b\in\mathbf Z$ satisfy $C^q=0$ whenever $q<a$ or $q>b$. If $C^q[0]\in\mathcal S$ for every $a\leq q\leq b$, then the image of $C^\bullet$ in $D(\mathcal A)$ belongs to $\mathcal S$. Here $C^q[0]$ denotes the single complex with term $C^q$ in degree zero. No retract closure, flatness, projectivity, or condition on the cohomology objects is assumed; the conclusion includes an empty support interval.

source.place: Tag 0FCP, lemma-K-bounded-derived, proof: the displayed stupid-truncation triangles and finite induction, extracted as a sublemma (not the K-group assertion).

proof.text: Write $Q$ for the localization functor of [def-weil-abstract-derived-category]. If $a>b$, every integer $q$ satisfies $q<a$ or $q>b$, so every $C^q$ is zero. Thus $C^\bullet$ is isomorphic to the zero complex and its image is zero in $D(\mathcal A)$, hence belongs to $\mathcal S$ by hypothesis. Now assume $a\le b$. For $n\in\mathbf Z$ define $T_n=\sigma_{\ge n}C$ by $T_n^q=C^q$ for $q\ge n$ and $T_n^q=0$ for $q<n$, with differential $d_C^q$ when $q\ge n$ and zero otherwise. The complex identities follow from $d_C^{q+1}d_C^q=0$; at a cut they are zero identities. The support bounds give $T_a\cong C^\bullet$ and $T_{b+1}\cong0$ by the termwise identity maps on nonzero terms and the unique maps on zero terms.

source.place: Tag 0FCP, lemma-K-bounded-derived, proof: displayed stupid-truncation triangles and finite induction (lines 9112–9128).

proof.text: For $a\le n\le b$, let $E_n$ be the complex with $C^n$ in degree $n$ and zero elsewhere. Define $i_n:T_{n+1}\to T_n$ to be the identity in degrees $q\ge n+1$ and zero below, and $p_n:T_n\to E_n$ to be the identity in degree $n$ and zero elsewhere. Both commute with differentials: away from the cut this is identity commutation or a zero identity, while at degree $n$ the inclusion has zero source and the projection has zero target in degree $n+1$. The sequence $0\to T_{n+1}\xrightarrow{i_n}T_n\xrightarrow{p_n}E_n\to0$ is degreewise short exact in the abelian category [def-sp-abelian]. In degree $n$ it is $0\to0\to C^n\xrightarrow{1}C^n\to0$; in degrees $q\ge n+1$ it is $0\to C^q\xrightarrow{1}C^q\to0\to0$; below $n$ every object is zero. Thus no assertion about truncations is being invoked without a proof.

source.place: Tag 0FCP, lemma-K-bounded-derived, proof: displayed stupid-truncation triangles and finite induction (lines 9112–9128).

proof.text: Apply [lem-weil-pbc-complex-ses-triangle] to the degreewise short exact sequence just constructed. Its hypotheses are exactly that $\mathcal A$ is abelian and $D(\mathcal A)$ exists, both assumed here. For every $a\le n\le b$ this gives a distinguished triangle $Q(T_{n+1})\to Q(T_n)\to Q(E_n)\to Q(T_{n+1})[1]$. Only existence and distinguishedness are needed; the boundary map's naturality and its sign play no role.

source.place: Tag 0FCP, lemma-K-bounded-derived, proof: displayed stupid-truncation triangles and finite induction (lines 9112–9128).

proof.text: The shift convention of [def-weil-abstract-derived-category] gives $E_n\cong C^n[0][-n]$: the unique nonzero term has degree $n$, and the shifted differential is zero regardless of its sign. Since $Q$ commutes with shifts, $Q(E_n)\cong Q(C^n[0])[-n]$. The hypothesis puts $Q(C^n[0])$ in $\mathcal S$ for $a\le n\le b$; closure under all integer shifts and isomorphisms, assumed in the statement, puts $Q(E_n)$ in $\mathcal S$ as well.

source.place: Tag 0FCP, lemma-K-bounded-derived, proof: displayed stupid-truncation triangles and finite induction (lines 9112–9128).

proof.text: Set $N=b-a+1\in\mathbf Z_{>0}$. Induct on integers $k=0,\ldots,N$ to prove $Q(T_{b+1-k})\in\mathcal S$. At $k=0$ this is the zero object identified in Step 1. For $k<N$, put $n=b-k$, so $a\le n\le b$ and $n+1=b+1-k$. The induction hypothesis gives the first vertex $Q(T_{n+1})$ of the distinguished triangle of Step 3, and Step 4 gives its third vertex $Q(E_n)$. For completeness, rotate this triangle twice using (TR2) of [def-weil-triangulated-category]. Its vertices are $Q(E_n),Q(T_{n+1})[1],Q(T_n)[1]$. The first two lie in $\mathcal S$ by Step 4 and shift closure, so third-vertex closure gives $Q(T_n)[1]\in\mathcal S$, and shifting by $[-1]$ gives $Q(T_n)\in\mathcal S$. This is the claim for $k+1$. At $k=N$ this is $Q(T_a)\in\mathcal S$. The isomorphism $T_a\cong C^\bullet$ from Step 1 and closure under isomorphisms finish the proof.
